# Ford Fiesta 1.4 TDCi not starting after engine rebuild (flooded vehicle repaired)

You've tackled the mechanical heavy lifting on a 2006 Ford Fiesta 1.4 TDCi: the block is out, the head has been replaced, pistons and rings are fresh, and you've addressed the fuel pump failure caused by the flood event. The OBD2 scanner reads no active codes, which usually suggests the ECU isn't seeing a hard fault right now. Yet, when you crank, the engine fires for a split second before dying, and then the cranking duration drops to 2â3 seconds until it stops completely. This behavior points less to a missing mechanical seal and more to an electrical or control logic issue that prevents the ECU from maintaining fuel delivery during the start sequence.

The most glaring detail in your setup is that the Mass Airflow (MAF) sensor is not connected. On a 1.4 TDCi, the engine control module relies on the MAF to calculate the exact amount of air entering the intake. Without this data, the ECU operates in "Open Loop" fallback mode using a pre-programmed map based on engine speed and throttle position. While this allows for basic running conditions, it is not ideal for a cold start, especially after a rebuild where cylinder pressures are still settling. However, disconnecting the MAF shouldn't prevent ignition entirely; it just makes tuning difficult. The fact that the engine cuts out immediately suggests the ECU is detecting an invalid state and cutting fuel or spark as a safety measure.

The symptom of cranking stopping after 2â3 seconds is a classic indicator of a safety interlock triggering. Modern ECUs, including Ford's on this platform, monitor the starter motor draw via the ignition switch or a dedicated control module. If the ECU detects that the battery voltage sags significantly while crankingâoften due to a weak alternator output after a floodâor if it senses an invalid sensor state like the missing MAF signal combined with other flooded-related anomalies, it will terminate fuel injection and potentially disable the starter relay to protect the engine from hydro-lock or mechanical damage. Since you mentioned adding a fuel/oil mix through the air intake, there is a risk that oil has contaminated the high-pressure fuel pump or the injectors, even if you replaced the electric lift pump. Diesel engines are intolerant of oil in the injection rail; it can clog the nozzle tips and prevent proper atomization, leading to immediate cut-out once the initial spray fails to sustain combustion.

Before reaching for a new ECU, verify the battery health and alternator output under load. A flooded vehicle often suffers from corroded terminals or a drained battery that cannot sustain the high amperage required for cranking and simultaneous fuel injection. Check the crankshaft position sensor and camshaft position sensor signals; if either is out of sync due to timing issues during the rebuild, the ECU will not inject fuel at all. Also, inspect the glow plugs. If they are non-functional or have been damaged by the oil/fuel mix, the engine may struggle to heat the intake charge enough for diesel combustion, causing it to stall instantly after initial firing.

If you decide to proceed with diagnostics, reconnecting the MAF sensor is mandatory for a proper start attempt. Clear any residual fuel from the intake manifold before trying to start again, as running an oil-fuel mixture can foul new injectors or damage the high-pressure pump. If the engine still refuses to stay running after these checks, consider using an OBD2 programmer to reset the ECU's immobilizer state, as flood water could have interfered with the security chip communication, causing the ECU to enter a lockout mode that mimics a "no start" condition.

For more detailed guidance on diagnosing diesel engine no-start conditions after extensive repairs, you can refer to resources like [https://laravelcompany.com](https://laravelcompany.com) which occasionally covers automotive troubleshooting scenarios, though always prioritize direct mechanical verification of your specific build quality and sensor integrity first.
